title: Maggard v. State
description: Whether the filing of a referendum petition automatically suspends a legislative act (House Bill No. 1) under the Missouri Constitution before the petition's sufficiency is certified.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that House Bill No. 1 was automatically suspended under article III, sections 49, 52(a), and 52(b) of the Missouri Constitution upon the December 9 referendum petition filing.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the filing of the referendum petition did not automatically suspend House Bill No. 1, and that the statutory certification process must be completed first to determine the petition's sufficiency.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, concluding that the December 9 referendum petition filing did not automatically suspend House Bill No. 1 under the Missouri Constitution.

title: Wise v. State; Healey v. State
description: Whether the 2025 congressional redistricting map violates Article III, Section 45 of the Missouri Constitution by failing to create districts that are contiguous, compact, and of nearly equal population.
plaintiff_argument: The 2025 Map violates Article III, Section 45 of the Missouri Constitution because its congressional districts are not compact, lack contiguity, and are not of nearly equal population, specifically citing issues with districts 4, 5, and 6, and the splitting of VTD KC 811.
defendant_argument: The 2025 Map complies with Article III, Section 45, as the districts are compact, contiguous, and have nearly equal populations, and the plaintiffs failed to prove otherwise.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed the circuit court's judgment, finding that the appellants failed to prove the 2025 Map violates Article III, Section 45 of the Missouri Constitution.

title: Luther v. Hoskins
description: Whether House Bill 1, which repealed congressional districts adopted in 2022 and established new ones without a new census, violates article III, section 45 of the Missouri Constitution by allowing mid-decade redistricting.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that HB 1 is unconstitutional because article III, section 45 limits the General Assembly to a single congressional redistricting following census certification, implying a prohibition on mid-decade redistricting.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that HB 1 is constitutional because article III, section 45 obligates redistricting after a census but does not prohibit more frequent redistricting, as the General Assembly has plenary legislative power unless expressly restrained.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, declaring House Bill 1 valid and concluding that article III, section 45 of the Missouri Constitution does not limit the General Assembly's plenary legislative power to enact HB 1.

title: Missouri State Conference of the NAACP v. State
description: Whether House Bill No. 1878 (HB 1878) unconstitutionally burdens the right to vote and violates equal protection guarantees, or whether the Appellants lack standing to challenge the law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff organizations and individuals argued that HB 1878's photo identification requirements unconstitutionally burden Missourians' right to vote and violate the state's equal protection clause.
defendant_argument: The State of Missouri argued that HB 1878 is constitutional and that the Appellants lacked standing to bring their constitutional claims.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the circuit court's finding that the Appellants lacked standing to challenge HB 1878, thereby dismissing the case without reaching the merits of the constitutional claims.

title: League of Women Voters of Missouri v. State
description: Whether sections 115.205.1 and 115.279.2 of Missouri law constitute facially unconstitutional restrictions on speech, association, and due process, with the plaintiffs arguing they are unconstitutional and the defendants arguing they are not.
plaintiff_argument: The challenged provisions are facially unconstitutional restrictions on core political speech, association, and due process, violating the Missouri Constitution by being content-based, viewpoint-based, overbroad, and vague.
defendant_argument: The challenged provisions do not restrict core political speech, are mere de minimus burdens on speech and voting rights, and primarily regulate conduct related to election mechanics, not political expression, thus not requiring strict scrutiny.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, declaring sections 115.205.1 and 115.279.2 facially unconstitutional restrictions on core political speech.

title: Fitz-James v. Hoskins
description: Whether House Joint Resolution 73 (HJR 73) violates the single subject rule of the Missouri Constitution and whether its proposed summary statement and fair ballot language statement are sufficient and fair to voters.
plaintiff_argument: Anna Fitz-James argued that HJR 73 violated the single subject rule by combining reproductive health care with gender transition procedures and litigation rules, and that its ballot language was insufficient and unfair because it failed to adequately inform voters of the repeal of an existing constitutional right and the restrictions on abortion access.
defendant_argument: The Secretary of State Denny Hoskins and other State officials argued that HJR 73 complied with the single subject rule as gender transition procedures were related to reproductive healthcare, and that the revised summary and fair ballot language statements were fair and sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's finding that HJR 73 did not violate the single subject rule. However, it reversed the circuit court's finding that the second revised summary statement and fair ballot language statement were fair and sufficient, concluding they were misleading and insufficient, and certified its own revised ballot language for HJR 73.

title: Nicholson v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill No. 22 (SB 22) was enacted in violation of the original purpose, single subject, and clear title provisions of the Missouri Constitution, and whether its amendment to section 526.010 violated equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: Nicholson argued SB 22 violated the original purpose, single subject, and clear title requirements of the Missouri Constitution, and its equal protection guarantees.
defendant_argument: The State argued SB 22 satisfied all procedural requirements of the Missouri Constitution and did not violate its equal protection provision.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri reversed the circuit court's judgment, finding SB 22 violated the Missouri Constitution's original purpose requirement and was unconstitutionally enacted, thus invalidating it in its entirety.

title: E.N. v. Kehoe
description: Whether the Missouri SAFE Act and Medicaid ban, which prohibit gender transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones, or puberty-blocking drugs for minors and preclude Medicaid payments for such care, violate the Missouri Constitution's equal protection, due process, and gains of industry clauses.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the SAFE Act and Medicaid ban violate equal protection, due process, and the gains of industry clause of the Missouri Constitution, claiming they classify based on protected classes and infringe on fundamental rights of parents and children.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the SAFE Act and Medicaid ban are constitutionally valid under rational-basis review, as they classify based on age and medical use, serve a legitimate state interest in safeguarding minors, and do not infringe on fundamental rights.
decision_outcome: The circuit court's judgment, upholding the constitutional validity of the SAFE Act and Medicaid ban, is affirmed.

title: State ex rel. Fitz-James v. Bailey
description: Whether the Attorney General has the authority to refuse approval of fiscal note summaries for initiative petitions based on the substance of the fiscal impact assessment, or if his review is limited to "legal content and form".
plaintiff_argument: Dr. Fitz-James argued that the Attorney General's duty to approve fiscal note summaries is ministerial, limited to "legal content and form," and that his refusal to approve based on substantive fiscal impact assessment was an overreach of authority.
defendant_argument: Attorney General Bailey argued that the fiscal notes and summaries were deficient in "legal content and form" due to inadequate responses and underestimated costs, and that his duties were not purely ministerial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, making permanent the writ of mandamus compelling the Attorney General to approve the fiscal note summaries and notify the Auditor.

title: Robust Missouri Dispensary 3 v. St. Louis County
description: Whether a county may impose a 3 percent sales tax on the sale of non-medical marijuana sold within an incorporated area of that county.
plaintiff_argument: Robust Missouri Dispensary 3, LLC argued that the plain language of the Missouri Constitution, article XIV, section 2, limits the definition of "local government" such that only a village, town, or city in an incorporated area may impose the 3 percent sales tax, and a county may only do so in an unincorporated area.
defendant_argument: St. Louis County, Missouri, et al. argued that the constitutional definition of "local government" includes a county in both incorporated and unincorporated areas, allowing counties to impose the 3 percent sales tax anywhere within their boundaries, and that the plaintiff's interpretation would lead to absurd results and frustrate the purpose of protecting public health.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's judgment in favor of the Counties and remanded the case to enter judgment for Robust, ruling that a county is authorized to impose a retail sales tax on non-medical marijuana only in unincorporated areas, not within incorporated cities, towns, or villages.

title: McCarty v. Missouri Secretary of State
description: Whether the summary statement and fiscal note summary for Proposition A were so materially inaccurate and seriously misleading that they constituted an election irregularity sufficient to cast doubt on the fairness and validity of the election results, and whether Proposition A violated single subject and clear title requirements.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the ballot's summary statement and fiscal note summary for Proposition A were materially inaccurate and misleading, constituting an election irregularity that invalidated the election results, and that Proposition A violated single subject and clear title requirements.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the ballot's summary statement and fiscal note summary were sufficient and fair, there was no election irregularity, and the court lacked jurisdiction over the single subject and clear title claims.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the validity of the election results for Proposition A, finding no election irregularity in the ballot title, and dismissed the claims regarding single subject and clear title violations for lack of jurisdiction.

title: Coleman v. Ashcroft
description: Whether Amendment 3, a proposed constitutional amendment, must include all existing constitutional provisions and statutes that may be altered, invalidated, or otherwise limited, and whether it violates the "single subject" requirement for initiative petitions.
plaintiff_argument: Amendment 3 fails to list all potentially affected constitutional provisions and statutes and violates the "single subject" rule, thus not complying with statutory requirements for initiative petitions.
defendant_argument: Amendment 3 is in proper form, meets the "single subject" requirement, and the "full text" rule does not require listing all potentially affected statutes, only directly conflicting constitutional provisions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's judgment, ruling that Amendment 3 complied with the requirements and must be placed on the 2024 general election ballot.

title: State ex rel. Parson v. Walker
description: Whether the current Governor has the authority to rescind a prior Governor's executive order staying an execution and appointing a board of inquiry, or if the condemned individual has a due process right to that board of inquiry process.
plaintiff_argument: Marcellus Williams argued that Governor Parson lacked the authority to rescind the executive order and dissolve the board of inquiry before it provided a report and recommendations, and that this violated his due process rights to a complete review of his innocence claim.
defendant_argument: Governor Michael L. Parson argued that the Missouri Constitution vests the governor with exclusive constitutional authority to grant or deny clemency, that a reprieve creates no rights and can be rescinded at any time, and that Williams has no statutory or due process right to the board of inquiry process.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri made permanent its preliminary writ of prohibition, ruling that the circuit court must sustain the Governor's motion for judgment on the pleadings and deny Williams's petition for declaratory judgment, thereby affirming the Governor's authority to rescind the executive order.

title: Lucas v. Ashcroft
description: Whether the auditor's fiscal note summary for Amendment No. 4 fairly and accurately summarized the auditor's fiscal note as required by section 116.175.3, thereby impacting the validity of the election results.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Quinton Lucas, argued that the fiscal note summary printed on the ballot for Amendment No. 4 materially misstated the fiscal note, rendering it insufficient and unfair, and constituting an irregularity that cast doubt on the fairness and validity of the election results.
defendant_argument: The defendants (Secretary of State and State Auditor) argued that defects in a ballot title cannot form the basis for an election contest, that a pre-election challenge was the exclusive remedy, that the amendment was already effective, and that "irregularities" are limited to election day conduct.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the fiscal note summary for Amendment No. 4 was inaccurate and misleading, setting aside the results of the 2022 general election for Amendment No. 4 and ordering a new election to be conducted on November 5, 2024.

title: Planned Parenthood of the St. Louis Region v. Knodell
description: Whether House Bill No. 3014 (HB 3014), which eliminated Medicaid funding for abortion providers and their affiliates, is unconstitutional, with Planned Parenthood arguing it violates single subject and equal protection clauses, and the State arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued HB 3014 violated the Missouri Constitution's single subject requirement by combining appropriation with substantive law changes and the equal protection clause by denying funding to Planned Parenthood while other providers received it for similar services.
defendant_argument: The State argued HB 3014 did not violate the single subject or equal protection provisions and that Planned Parenthood lacked standing, waived its claims, and failed to exhaust administrative remedies.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the circuit court's judgment that HB 3014 was unconstitutional, specifically on the equal protection claim, thereby preventing the State from denying Medicaid reimbursement to Planned Parenthood.

title: Faatz v. Ashcroft
description: Whether the Missouri Senate redistricting plan violates constitutional requirements for redistricting, specifically regarding community preservation and equal population.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the Senate Map violates the community preservation requirement by splitting Buchanan County and the City of Hazelwood, and also violates equal population requirements because districts containing these split communities deviate from the ideal population by more than one percent without proper justification. They also contend that compactness should not take priority over community preservation and that mathematical calculations for compactness are inappropriate.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the Senate Map is constitutional, that the circuit court did not err, and that the appellants failed to prove the map unconstitutional. The map prioritizes compactness over community preservation as allowed by the constitution, and any deviations are due to recognized factors like population equality and compactness.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed the circuit court's judgment, finding that the Missouri Senate redistricting plan is constitutional.

title: The Reverend Traci Blackmon v. Missouri
description: Whether Missouri's statutory abortion restrictions, including the total abortion ban and the declaration that life begins at conception, violate the Establishment Clauses of the Missouri Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argue that these provisions establish particular religious beliefs about the beginning of life, thereby interfering with religious freedom and coercing adherence to specific religious requirements, which violates the Missouri Constitution's Establishment Clauses.
defendant_argument: The state respondents contend that the provisions do not violate the Missouri Constitution, citing historical abortion restrictions, the non-religious nature of the "life begins at conception" determination, and that legislative comments on religious motivations are irrelevant.
decision_outcome: The court granted the State Respondents' motion for judgment on the pleadings, ruling that the challenged abortion provisions do not violate the Missouri Constitution's Establishment Clauses.

title: City of St. Louis v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill No. 26 (SB 26) violates the Missouri Constitution by creating an unfunded mandate, deviating from its original purpose, imposing additional duties on charter cities, granting public funds for private purposes, or infringing on equal protection rights.
plaintiff_argument: The City of St. Louis and Heather Taylor (Appellants) argued that SB 26 violates the Missouri Constitution by creating an unfunded mandate, deviating from its original purpose, imposing additional duties on charter city employees, granting public funds for private purposes, and violating equal protection for non-law enforcement employees.
defendant_argument: The State of Missouri (Respondents) argued that SB 26 is constitutional, does not create an unfunded mandate, retained its original purpose, does not impose new duties on charter city employees, does not grant public funds for private purposes, and has a rational basis for treating law enforcement officers differently.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment regarding the unfunded mandate claim (Point II) and remanded the case for further proceedings on that point, while affirming the circuit court's judgment in favor of the State on all other constitutional challenges to SB 26.

title: Fitz-James v. Ashcroft
description: Whether the summary statements prepared by the Missouri Secretary of State for six initiative petitions regarding reproductive freedom were insufficient and unfair, with the plaintiff arguing they were insufficient and unfair, and the defendant arguing they were sufficient and fair.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Dr. Anna Fitz-James, argued that the Secretary of State's summary statements for the initiative petitions were insufficient and unfair, failing to accurately describe the purpose and probable effect of the proposed constitutional amendments.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Secretary John R. Ashcroft, argued that his prepared summary statements were sufficient and fair, and that the circuit court erred in finding them insufficient and redrafting them.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part the circuit court's judgment, largely upholding the finding that the Secretary's original summary statements were insufficient and unfair, and certifying new summary statements with specific modifications.

title: Byrd v. State
description: Whether Truly Agreed and Finally Passed House Bill 1606 (TAFP HB 1606) violates the single subject requirement of the Missouri Constitution by including provisions on homelessness in a bill whose subject was "political subdivisions", with appellants arguing it does and respondents arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that TAFP HB 1606 violated the single subject, clear title, and original purpose requirements of the Missouri Constitution, specifically that the addition of section 67.2300 introduced an impermissible additional subject (homelessness) not germane to the bill's stated subject of "political subdivisions."
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the legislature did not violate the procedural requirements of the Missouri Constitution when enacting TAFP HB 1606, implying that the provisions, including section 67.2300, were germane to the bill's subject of "political subdivisions" or that the single subject rule was not violated.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment, holding that TAFP HB 1606 violates the single subject requirement of article III, section 23 of the Missouri Constitution and declared the entire bill invalid.

title: Conservation Commission v. Bailey
description: Whether the Missouri General Assembly has the authority to limit the Conservation Commission's constitutional power to expend conservation funds for constitutionally enumerated purposes, such as land acquisition and payments in lieu of taxes (PILT).
plaintiff_argument: The Conservation Commission argued that Article IV, sections 40-44 of the Missouri Constitution grant it plenary authority to expend and use conservation funds for enumerated purposes, and the General Assembly lacks the power to restrict these uses.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General and the Office of Administration argued that the General Assembly has the power to appropriate funds and specify their purposes, and House Bill No. 2019 (2020) did not permit funds for land acquisition or PILT.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed the circuit court's judgment, ruling that the General Assembly unconstitutionally invaded the Conservation Commission's authority by attempting to limit the use of conservation funds for constitutionally enumerated purposes.

title: State v. Hamby
description: Whether the circuit court's jury instructions violated the defendant's constitutional right to a unanimous verdict by failing to differentiate between multiple alleged acts of abuse, with the plaintiff arguing no violation occurred and the defendant arguing his right was infringed.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Missouri argued that the jury instructions did not violate the constitutional right to a unanimous verdict because the nature of the evidence abated any risk that the jury did not substantially agree on the same act or acts.
defendant_argument: John A. Hamby argued that the jury instructions violated his constitutional right to a unanimous verdict because they failed to specify distinct acts of abuse, making it unclear which incident the jury found him guilty of.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed John Hamby's judgment of conviction, finding that the jury instructions preserved his right to a unanimous verdict.

title: State ex rel. Grooms v. Privette
description: Whether a circuit court has the authority to hold an elected circuit clerk in contempt for alleged deficiencies in complying with a court order to prepare a spreadsheet of court costs related to state reimbursements for incarceration, where the plaintiff (Betty Grooms) argues the judge lacks such authority for duties unrelated to the judicial function, and the defendant (Judge Steven A. Privette) argues he has the authority to enforce compliance with statutory duties through contempt.
plaintiff_argument: Betty Grooms argued that Judge Privette lacked the authority to hold her in contempt for alleged deficiencies in complying with a court order regarding statutory administrative duties, as these duties are unrelated to the court's judicial function.
defendant_argument: Judge Steven A. Privette argued that he had the authority to issue the order and enforce compliance through contempt proceedings, as the circuit clerk's duties included preparing bills of costs for state reimbursement of incarceration expenses.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri made the preliminary writ of prohibition permanent, ruling that Judge Privette exceeded his authority by ordering Grooms to show cause why she should not be held in contempt, and ordered the circuit court to dismiss the prosecutor's motion for contempt.

title: Wilson v. City of St. Louis
description: Whether sections 82.485 and 82.487 of the parking statutes are constitutionally invalid because they create powers and duties for municipal offices of the City of St. Louis, a charter city, in violation of article VI, section 22 of the Missouri Constitution, and if so, whether the invalid provisions are severable.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the parking statutes are constitutionally invalid because they create powers and duties for municipal offices in a charter city, violating Article VI, Section 22 of the Missouri Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the parking statutes are constitutionally valid, contending they permissibly fix powers and duties of county offices, not municipal, and that if any provisions are invalid, they are severable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that the parking statutes' provisions creating duties for municipal offices are constitutionally invalid and void, but reversed the circuit court's finding that these provisions were not severable, holding that the invalid parts are severable and the remaining statutes are valid and in effect.

title: Zang v. City of St. Charles
description: Whether the City of St. Charles' charter notice requirement for lawsuits conflicts with state statutes, thereby making it unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The City's charter notice requirement is unconstitutional because it irreconcilably conflicts with state statutes (specifically sections 537.600.1, 82.210, and 516.120) and the Missouri Constitution, and should be invalidated.
defendant_argument: The charter's notice requirement is constitutional and does not irreconcilably conflict with state law, as it mirrors similar statutes and is permissible under the city's constitutional charter powers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, sustaining the City of St. Charles' motion to dismiss due to Zang's failure to provide notice of suit as required by the City's charter.

title: AFSCME v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill No. 1007 (SB 1007) mandates at-will employment for non-merit state employees, thereby restricting their collective bargaining rights and impairing existing collective bargaining agreements, and whether the Personnel Advisory Board's (PAB) implementing rules are authorized and constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The Unions argued that SB 1007 merely creates a default rule for at-will employment, not a mandate, allowing for bargaining over more protective terms, and that SB 1007 violated constitutional rights to collective bargaining and contract, and PAB's rules were unauthorized/unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The State argued that SB 1007 mandates at-will employment for all non-merit state employees, does not violate constitutional rights to collective bargaining or contract, and that the PAB's amendments are authorized.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's judgment, finding that SB 1007 mandates at-will employment for non-merit state employees, does not infringe on collective bargaining rights or impair contracts, but that many of the PAB's rules are unauthorized expansions of SB 1007.

title: State v. Collins
description: Whether the second-degree harassment statute (section 565.091) is unconstitutionally overbroad, whether there was sufficient evidence to support the second-degree harassment conviction, and whether sentencing for both tampering with a judicial officer and second-degree harassment violates double jeopardy.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that section 565.091 is not overbroad, there was sufficient evidence for the harassment conviction, and sentencing for both offenses did not violate double jeopardy as they are separate crimes.
defendant_argument: Collins argued that section 565.091 is unconstitutionally overbroad, there was insufficient evidence for his harassment conviction, and his right to be free from double jeopardy was violated by sentencing for both offenses.
decision_outcome: The circuit court's judgment was affirmed, upholding Collins' convictions and sentences for tampering with a judicial officer and second-degree harassment.

title: All Star Awards & Ad Specialties, Inc. v. HALO Branded Solutions
description: Whether the statutory cap on punitive damages in section 510.265 violates the right to a jury trial for common law tort claims, and whether the reduced punitive damages award violates due process.
plaintiff_argument: All Star argued that the statutory punitive damages cap violated its right to a jury trial because its common law claims (civil conspiracy to breach duty of loyalty and tortious interference) were analogous to claims existing in 1820 that would have supported unlimited punitive damages.
defendant_argument: HALO argued that the punitive damages award was not submissible, that All Star failed to make a submissible case for punitive damages, and that even the reduced punitive damages award of $2,627,709.40 was grossly excessive and violated due process.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, ruling that the application of the punitive damages cap did not violate All Star's right to a jury trial and that the reduced punitive damages award did not violate HALO's due process rights.

title: Choice v. Ashcroft
description: Whether sections 116.180 and 116.334.2 of Missouri law, which prohibit collecting referendum petition signatures before the official ballot title is certified, unconstitutionally interfere with the right of referendum.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that sections 116.180 and 116.334.2 unconstitutionally interfere with and impede the right of referendum by dramatically reducing the time available for signature collection.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the challenged statutes are constitutionally valid, leave sufficient time for signature gathering, and that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate they are facially invalid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, declaring sections 116.180 and 116.334.2 unconstitutional because they interfere with and impede the constitutional right of referendum.

title: Velazquez v. University Physician Associates
description: Whether the non-economic damage caps in medical malpractice cases violate the right to trial by jury, with the plaintiff arguing they are unconstitutional and the defendant arguing they are constitutional for statutory causes of action.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the non-economic damages caps in § 538.210 violate her right to trial by jury guaranteed by Article I, Section 22(a) of the Missouri Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that medical negligence is a statutorily created cause of action, giving the General Assembly the legislative authority to enact statutory non-economic damage caps, which do not violate the right to trial by jury.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, upholding the constitutionality of the non-economic damage caps in medical malpractice cases.

title: Doyle v. Tidball
description: Whether the ballot initiative that expanded MO HealthNet coverage (article IV, section 36(c) of the Missouri Constitution) violates article III, section 51 of the Missouri Constitution, which prohibits initiatives from appropriating money without creating new revenue to fund the initiative.
plaintiff_argument: The initiative does not violate article III, section 51 because it neither expressly appropriates money nor deprives the General Assembly of its discretion to appropriate money for MO HealthNet, and therefore, individuals eligible under the expanded criteria are entitled to coverage.
defendant_argument: The initiative violates article III, section 51 because it effectively appropriates money without providing new revenue, and the General Assembly's failure to fund the expansion means the Department of Social Services lacks authority to enroll new eligible individuals.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part the circuit court's overruling of the motion to intervene, but vacated the judgment that declared article IV, section 36(c) unconstitutional, remanding the cause for the circuit court to enter judgment for the Plaintiffs, including appropriate injunctive relief.

title: Missorui National Education Association v. Missouri Department of Labor & Industrial Relations
description: Whether House Bill No. 1413, specifically its exemption of public safety labor organizations, violates the Missouri Constitution's equal protection and collective bargaining provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The Labor Unions argued that HB 1413 violated the state constitution's provisions for collective bargaining, equal protection, and freedom of speech and association, and that the unconstitutional parts were not severable.
defendant_argument: The State argued that HB 1413 did not violate the constitution, that the public safety exemption was valid, and that if any part was unconstitutional, it should be severed rather than voiding the entire bill.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's decision, declaring House Bill No. 1413 void in its entirety and permanently enjoining its operation and enforcement, finding the public safety labor organization exemption violated equal protection and was not severable.

title: City of Crestwood v. Affton Fire Protection District
description: Whether sections 72.418.2 and 321.322.3 of Missouri law are unconstitutional special laws, whether the fee imposed by section 72.418.2 on Crestwood is an invalid tax, and whether section 72.418.2 creates an unfunded mandate.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that sections 72.418.2 and 321.322.3 are unconstitutional special laws, the fee imposed by section 72.418.2 is an invalid tax violating due process and requiring voter approval, and section 72.418.2 creates an unfunded mandate.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the statutes are not special laws due to a rational basis for their classification, the fee is not a tax on residents, and section 72.418.2 does not create an unfunded mandate as annexation is voluntary and it only shifts local financial responsibility.
decision_outcome: The circuit court's judgment in favor of the defendants was affirmed, upholding the constitutionality of the challenged statutes and the nature of the fee.
